newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia finds funds for Alpha space station.
newsitem.headline: Russia finds funds for Alpha space station.

text.p: The Russian space agency said on Tuesday it has raised the money to build the basic module of the Alpha space station, problems with which have cast doubts on Moscow's participation in the international project.
Agency chief Yuri Koptev told a news conference on Tuesday that four private Russian banks would offer an 800 billion rouble ($140 million) loan to the agency.
The Finance Ministry has held a tender to choose four banks among 24 who wanted to finance the project," Koptev said. The loan formalities would be completed by May 15.
Koptev said Russia was still a vital part of the project and had overcome financial difficulties which have raised eyebrows among its Western partners.

"Russia's departure would throw the whole project two years behind schedule," Koptev said. He said Russia had been invited to meet its international partners on May 31 in Tokyo to discuss the project.
A final agreement on Alpha, involving Russia, the United States, the European Space Agency, Canada, Italy and Japan, will be signed next July in Denver, he said.
"This document will formalise Russia's participation in the Alpha project," he said.

He said the 480-tonne Alpha would probably cost $90-100 billion after all its 36 modules are assembled in orbit early in the next century. Alpha will replace Russia's 11 year-old Mir orbiting station.
Russia has undertaken to build 12 Alpha modules for $3.2 billion, and the United States plans to built 18 modules worth $17.2 billion, Koptev said.

Koptev said Russia's financial picture was improving, after the government promised in April to find a total of 1.5 trillion roubles to fund construction of the basic service module, where cosmonauts will work and live.
The station will have three parts, built by the United States and Russia, in its first stage.
"If we get the money we will meet our obligations," Koptev said. He said he hoped Russia would launch the service module in late December 1998.
Western partners had questioned whether Moscow was able to take part in the space station project after it said recently it could not afford to build the service module.
"We were in a very difficult situation over the last two years, when our Western partners were witnessing our insolvency," Koptev said.

Russia's Khrunichev space centre, which was paid $190 million by Boeing to build a storage module, one of the three anchor parts of Alpha, was negotiating a new contract to modify the station since design changes have been made, he said.
Koptev said the storage module known as the FGB, one of the three anchor parts, and the first to be put into space, would be launched in June 1998.
